records.name: Marshall Islands
records.summary:
The Marshall Islands demands real caution — from thin evidence rather than documented risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (decriminalised in the 2000s), there is no legal gender recognition, and no anti-trans pattern is documented; no LGBT-specific abuses were reported in the 2015 official human-rights report.

Caveat: the population is very small and the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust global criminalisation history: lists the Marshall Islands among the states that decriminalised same-sex conduct in the 2000s — "Marshall Islands (2005)" alongside USA (2003), Cape Verde (2004) and San Marino (2004) — i.e. no current criminalisation regime there.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Marshall Islands: significant problems were prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence; no reports of torture, arbitrary killings or disappearances - no LGBT-specific abuses reported.

Pacific Sexual & Gender Diversity Network Marshall Islands page: profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga ("Nenol"), 25, a pansexual genderqueer Marshallese who co-created and led "Brighten the Rainbow", known as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands; also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.

records.name: Benin
records.summary: Benin is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline — legal but entirely unshielded, no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

records.name: Togo
records.summary: Togo is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “immodest or unnatural acts” (3 years); limited recent enforcement evidence but documented discrimination and violence; no LGR.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile (fetched this session): Togo criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine — the core exposure fact for a visitor.

AAEC Togo + Synergia alternative report to the UN Human Rights Committee (June 2021): the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal/judicial support to victims — evidence of an active civil-society documentation and assistance channel.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Togo: the law prohibits 'acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex' (widely understood as same-sex conduct) and also the 'promotion of same-sex conduct', reaching advocacy and gender identity expression; the law was enforced, and violence/threats targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues — official current-law + enforcement read.

Washington Blade (Aug 31, 2015): interviews with LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria (conducted 14-31 March 2015) include a Togo section — the author returned to Lomé, visited the site of a 2008 attack on him, and reports the capital's police are 'particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists', a rare on-the-ground note naming TOURIST exposure.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Togo: documents security-force torture, impunity, and 'official and societal discrimination... against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Togo: significant issues include cruel treatment, harsh prisons, arbitrary detention, criminal libel enforcement, and 'crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual...' persons.

records.name: Niger
records.summary: Niger is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News live page (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region — weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. Documents the legislative trail into the 2025 criminalisation.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men — including high-ranking military officials — imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026, in what campaigners describe as a 'witch-hunt' with a 'toxic' climate; sources also fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses. Current enforcement evidence for the record.

Agence Nigérienne de Presse (state news agency, French): headline 'Le Niger criminalise la Pratique LGBTQIA+ dans le pays' — official state-press announcement of the criminalisation. Page body was largely navigation content at fetch time; headline finding only.
